Kurt Gödel left 1,009 pages of densely written text – much of it in an obsolete shorthand – which is now said to contain hundreds of proved theorems
The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems , published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.
After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.
Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it.
Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about.
The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.
“I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.”
Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation.
In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978.

items.title: More Than 3,000 Tarantulas Were Found Hidden in Socks During a Major Wildlife Trafficking Bust at an Airport in Lima, Peru
items.desc: According to Peruvian officials, the three European travelers—including one who's been identified as a "renowned tarantula researcher"—could have made around $1.68 million from the creepy-crawly loot
items.text:
Authorities in Peru say they have foiled a plot to smuggle more than 3,000 tarantulas—including species not yet described in scientific publications—out of the country.
After receiving an anonymous tip , officials intercepted three travelers—two German citizens and one Polish citizen—at Jorge Chávez International Airport in Lima as they were checking in at the boarding area. When they searched the travelers’ luggage, they found thousands of eggs, hatchlings and adult spiders hidden in socks, according to a November 4 statement from the National Forest and Wildlife Service of Peru (SERFOR).
“We noticed that some of them were moving,” Cora Suárez , a SERFOR forest and wildlife control technician who works at the airport, tells the Agence France-Presse . “There were small ones and large ones.”
Workers used slender wooden sticks to gently brush the spiders into clear plastic containers. Once officials are done investigating them, the tarantulas will be taken to an authorized breeding center.
The travelers were trying to fly to Germany. Instead, they were detained by the Peruvian National Police’s environmental crimes unit and now face criminal charges.
Officials have not released the names of the individuals. However, one of the travelers was a “renowned tarantula researcher,” according to the statement, per a translation by the New York Times ’ Amanda Holpuch.
Authorities suspect the individuals were smuggling the spiders for private collections, research and the exotic pet trade. Suárez tells the AFP that one tarantula can sell for roughly $560 in Europe, meaning the smugglers could have made around $1.68 million from the more than 3,000 tarantulas they had hidden in their suitcases.
The spiders originated from several different parts of Peru, including the cities of Cajamarca, Cusco and Junín, and the regions of La Libertad and Loreto. Officials are still trying to pinpoint all the species in the loot but said it included several brightly colored creatures.
Wildlife trafficking is the world’s fourth-largest form of organized crime, with an estimated annual value of up to $20 billion .
So far, officials have identified Thrixopelma lagunas , also known as the Peruvian blue zebra or the blue birdeater. Authorities also found members of the Pamphobeteus genus, which are among the largest tarantulas in the world.

A charming drawing of a kingfisher by 13-year-old Prince George is featured in a special edition of Country Life magazine, revealing his artistic talents. Young George created the colored pencil illustration when he was just 12 years old last spring. The artwork is included as part of a wider 300-page special edition of the magazine that was guest edited by his father, the Prince of Wales.
It seems a love of art runs in the royal family. George’s grandfather, King Charles III, is a talented painter, while his mother, Catherine, Princess of Wales, and uncle, Harry, the Duke of Sussex, both studied art at A-level. Catherine later continued her studies in art history at St Andrews University in Scotland.
According to Country Life , Prince George has a “growing curiosity about the natural world.” His mother, Catherine, has similarly spoken about the comfort and healing she has found in nature during her recovery from cancer. She also discusses her personal journey in the special edition’s feature interview, where she recalls being warned that there would be “good days and bad days.”
Prince George and his siblings often make time to be creative. In 2025, the family released portrait sketches they drew of each other on social media. items.title: Archaeologists in England Discovered 8,000 Roman-Era Frog Bones in a Single Ditch. They Just Solved the Mystery of How the Amphibians Ended Up There
items.desc: New research suggests that medium-sized birds of prey such as short-eared owls feasted on the frogs during a "short, intensive predation event" some 1,700 years ago
items.text:
Meilan Solly | Senior Associate Digital Editor, History
Between 2016 and 2022, archaeologists conducting excavations along a planned stretch of England’s A14 highway unearthed an array of astonishing discoveries , including a Roman amulet carved to resemble the mythical Gorgon Medusa , the earliest physical evidence of beer production in Britain and an Iron Age comb crafted from a human skull.
Comprising more than 280,000 artifacts, the finds—uncovered between modern-day Cambridge and Huntingdon —shed light on life in the region over roughly 12,000 years. But some discoveries raised more questions than answers: Why, for example, did a single ditch at the Bar Hill site in rural Cambridgeshire contain some 8,000 amphibian bones ?
As Vicki Ewens , a senior zooarchaeologist at the Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA), told the Observer ’s Dalya Alberge in 2022, “In my experience, mainly working on sites from London, we don’t get that many frogs . To have so many bones coming from one ditch is extraordinary.”
Ewens and her colleagues outlined several possible explanations for the unusual cache. Perhaps the amphibians fell into the ditch (also described as a gully) and found themselves trapped. Or maybe they succumbed to extreme cold during their wintertime hibernation . Alternatively, they could have served as the centerpiece of a meal—or several—enjoyed by Iron Age humans, although the absence of cut marks on the bones rendered this scenario unlikely.
Four years after MOLA first announced the find, experts have finally solved the mystery of the ancient animal cemetery. Based on a groundbreaking analysis of amphibian arm bones, researchers led by Ewens and Paul Clarkson , an archaeologist at England’s Bournemouth University, concluded that most of the frogs whose remains were found in the ditch died young, eaten by birds of prey such as short-eared owls and hen harriers in the second or third century C.E., during Britain’s Roman era .
A combination of environmental factors and human activity produced ideal conditions for this avian feast to unfold over a relatively short timeframe. As the authors write in the journal Environmental Archaeology , water levels in the Fens —the marshy wetland that houses the gully—retreated during the Roman period, enabling frogs in drying-out ponds to reproduce at a faster rate. items.text:
During a Major League Baseball game between the Kansas City Royals and the Toronto Blue Jays, the best team performance didn’t take place on the field. Instead, it happened in the stands, where fans from all walks of life came together for a mouthwatering mission. All they had to do was to assemble an oversized, inflatable hot dog in a race against time.
The contest, known as “Home Bun Race,” was set up by QuickTrip, a chain of convenience stores in Midwestern, Southern, and Western United States. The objective is for fans in attendance to piece together a 10-foot-tall inflatable hot dog and equally sized bun, which were each launched from opposite sides of the stadium. If the crowd managed to unite the massive meal in under 35 seconds, there would be free hot dogs for everyone.
Though it sounds pretty straight forward, it can be tricky to coordinate and move the inflatable pieces in such a short amount of time—especially when it’s a crowd of strangers who haven’t prepared or ever worked together before. Still, the fans managed to achieve their goal, resulting in a World Series-level roar from the crowd. Although the home team lost 4-3, the fans walked away with a coupon that they could later redeem for their free treat. So… everyone won.
According to Ads of the World , QuickTrip created this campaign in partnership with Laughlin Constable, their creative and media agency. It is also the first activation of its kind in MLB, and the most successful social activation QuickTrip has ever done due to its social media reach and press coverage. In addition to Kauffman Stadium in Kansas City, the campaign has also taken place at the Cardinals stadium in St. Louis.

items.text:
A new generation of trash bins are aimed at conserving Japanese civic culture while addressing one of the country’s largest tourism headaches.
Solar-powered compactors and robots that haul trash away from key tourist areas are two such solutions already receiving a positive response.
If you’ve ever visited Japan, you too may have been left confused and eventually frustrated by what appears to be a total absence of public waste bins. This is by design.
Officials concerned about security and overflowing bins have left the public with few places to dispose of their trash. There is also a philosophy that if waste is difficult to dispose of, people will be less prone to creating it.
Japanese tourism authorities are beginning to understand that, while this approach may have seen citizens keep their streets clean for decades, it’s a major inconvenience for visitors.
Yet the trend towards removing waste bins has continued, with the Tokyo metro removing all public waste bins as recently as 2022. In parallel, however, the city has been enlisting the help of various firms to design smarter waste bins that hold more and won’t overflow.
One example is Forcetec, which sells and installs solar-powered waste bins developed in the United States called SmaGO. It compacts waste every 5 minutes and can hold 5 times as much trash as a non-compacting bin.
“There are many places that recognize the need for trash bins but hesitate to install them because they’re worried the bins will overflow or because of the labor required to collect the rubbish,” says Rina Ogata, a spokesperson for Forcetec.
“You can install SmaGO and reduce the frequency of rubbish collection. The communications function also allows operators to check online how full each bin is, so they can make collections more efficiently before the bins reach capacity.”
Companies like Forcetec have donated or subsidized these products as part of “a corporate hometown tax program” and “corporate sponsorships” according to Japan Times .
Another reason why cities like Kyoto and Tokyo decided to trash their trash cans was that they fill up too quickly in busy areas, and collection of each bin was an expensive outlay.
But what if the trash cans could collect themselves? Enter California-based firm Cartken , whose 40-liter robotic trash bins use sensors to measure when they’re almost full, at which point they drive themselves out of the public reach for emptying.

In 1994, David vacationed on the Greek island of Kos with his family for a memorable week in which the English teen met a new pen pal.
There were 12 kids, all from different families, that became a friendly pack. One of them was Jodie, who was 15 at the time.
“You know how kids hang out on holiday, we were all just around the pool table and we decided to swap addresses and be pen pals.”
“Me and Jodie were the only ones that stayed in contact—and we carried on writing to each other for years. A letter every month or so, catching up.”
But after three years of communication, David moved, and the pair lost contact.
Little did they know that 29 years later they would get married.
David McArdle from Newcastle was two years older than Jodie, and they both went on their separate life paths.
It wasn’t until twenty years later that David saw a text message arrive on his mother’s phone from Jodie, saying ‘Happy birthday from me and the girls’.
“I couldn’t believe I found her again,” David told Talk to the Press. “I said to my mum, ‘I didn’t know you had Jodie’s number.’”
He replied to the text immediately (saying it was David) and, after a nail-biting 15-minute wait, Jodie, a teaching assistant, messaged back.
“She said she was so glad to hear from me.
“It turns out, that 15-minute wait for her reply was because she was sobbing her heart out looking at the text. She’d wanted to get in touch, but she thought I was in a relationship so she didn’t want to ruffle any feathers.”
From then on, the two never stop talking on the phone for two years, before eventually meeting in person, for the first time in 24 years, when David drove 300 miles to Cardiff to visit Jodie.
“We sat on the sofa and talked for 12 hours,” recalled David who visited her again two weeks later.
After three years of dating, David proposed at the top of the London Eye Ferris wheel and the pair were soon married.
Now the couple live together in Cardiff but visit Kos, the island they met on, every year in August, back to the apartments where they met and swapped addresses.

items.title: Flood victim, 95, lived in Wetherspoons until she died after her home was destroyed
items.desc: Jean Powell kept asking when she could go back to her flat, which was flooded when the River Monnow burst its banks.
items.text:
Jean Powell was temporarily staying in one of Monmouth Wetherspoons' guest rooms while her flat was being refurbished after it was flooded a year ago
When neighbours hammered on Jean Powell's door and evacuated her to safety because the nearby river had burst its banks and swamped her town, little did she know she would never return home.
Jean sought a 10-month refuge at her local Wetherspoons but kept asking when she could go back to her flat, which was flooded when the River Monnow hit 18-times its normal level in south Wales in November 2025 .
But the 95-year-old never got to go back home and died in September - one of those who suffered a personal toll from the effects of being flooded.
"Jean used to say, when am I going home?" said friend and neighbour Wyn Smith. "All she wanted to do was come back home and we couldn't fulfil that."
The BBC report from last year when Monmouth town centre was hit by severe flooding after Storm Claudia
Jean was forced out of her home when the river hit record levels in the early hours of 15 November as a major incident was declared after almost a month's worth of rain fell in 24 hours.
It has officially been described as a one-in-75-year event when the river flooded more than 400 properties in the Welsh town during Storm Claudia - and overwhelmed the defences that were built 35 years ago to protect the centre of town.
Jean, like many in the small town near the Wales and England border, was rescued and after sleeping the night on her neighbour's chair sought temporary sanctuary in Monmouth's Wetherspoons as she had no close family to look after her.
"She was happy in the beginning because she was in town where she wanted to be," recalled Wyn, who visited her friend most days who was staying in one of The Kings Head's hotel rooms.
"The Wetherspoons staff were brilliant with Jean, they'd take her food and really looked after her."

An 81-year-old Englishman grew up wondering who his real father was. What he didn’t know was that an entire family tree in Canada was wondering who and where he was.
After being divided by a world war, an ocean, and 8 decades, Rodney Anderson has finally found his long lost relatives with the help of a simple DNA test, and a persistent, curious niece.
“I thought ‘This is a wind up.’ It has to be,” Anderson said, sharing with CBC News the moment he learned of his true origins.
“But it wasn’t. You can’t believe what a shock it is to get that knowledge.”
Anderson’s mother had a child with a visiting Canadian soldier during the Second World War, a secret that his mother and grandmother never shared with him.
He grew up with no knowledge or explanation of his father’s origins whatsoever because of the stigma attached at the time to these out-of-wedlock births, even though they came about during a period of immense crisis and uncertainty about the future.
Canadian Bethany Allen began searching in 2008 for this mystery uncle of hers after discovering in divorce papers that her grandfather, Charles Blakney, had had a child with a woman in the UK in 1944.
He had first sailed off to war in 1942, leaving behind a wife and daughter in New Brunswick. Blakney served as a motor and driver mechanic with the New Brunswick Rangers and returned home in 1945, the same year that Rodney Anderson was born in Farnham to his mother Yvonne. Rumors of his affair overseas remained in the family long after the guns fell silent in Europe.
“My mother [Rodney’s half-sister] had always wanted to know that [Anderson] had a good life and was happy,” Bethany Allen told CBC News.
It took a long time to confirm the link between the Blakney family in Canada and Anderson in Surrey. It came about through a commercial DNA test from Ancestry.

Alfred James Towle Taylor, an engineer with an interest in creating a bridge from the First Narrows to the North Shore, managed to convince the Guinness family of Dublin, Ireland to invest in the project. The bridge was designed by the Montreal firm Monsarrat and Pratley, which was later responsible for the Angus L. Macdonald Bridge in Halifax, Nova Scotia, using a similar design.
With a plebiscite vote agreeing on the project, it was completed in just 5 years under the shadow of the Great Depression. Like true gentlemen the Guinness family sold the bridge in 1955 to the province of British Columbia for $5,873,837—the cost of the original construction at not a penny more in appreciation.

Exclusive: investigation finds prescriptions for children under 12, as experts stress need for specialist supervision and long-term monitoring
Hundreds of children in England are receiving prescriptions for GLP-1 medications, including some younger than 12, the Guardian can reveal.
GLP-1 medications were initially developed to help people with type 2 diabetes control their blood sugar levels, but have since become a popular slimming aid, with products such as Wegovy and Mounjaro becoming household names.
While social media is awash with adults who have lost weight with GLP-1s, data shows a number of children are also being prescribed them.
A Guardian investigation has revealed that in the financial year 2025-26 there were 419 children under the age of 18 receiving such prescriptions, 10 of whom were under the age of 12. And in the four months to July this year, 341 children received GLP-1 prescriptions, 15 of whom were under the age of 12.
The figures, obtained from the NHS Business Services Authority through freedom of information requests, relate to prescriptions in England and dispensed in a community setting anywhere in the UK.
However, they do not cover those prescribed and dispensed via private prescriptions, in prisons, and in hospitals, meaning the figures are likely to be a considerable underestimate.
One private clinic for children has previously revealed it has more than 200 patients receiving the jabs. It is also unclear whether the GLP-1 figures reflect medications that are being given primarily for weight loss.
Martin Whyte, a professor of metabolic medicine at the University of Surrey, said the number of prescriptions was still small relative to the scale of childhood obesity, but those taking the drugs needed long-term change to their lifestyles.
He said: “The important thing is that children who start them do so within specialist services, with support for diet, growth and wellbeing, and a plan for the long term.
“That includes regular monitoring of growth and puberty, nutritional intake, mental health and eating behaviours, and side effects. This matters partly because we know weight tends to return when the drugs are stopped, and partly because we still have limited data on use over many years in growing young people.”

items.title: These London Apartments Look Straight Out of the Stone Age. Could They Be the Future of Sustainable Architecture?
items.desc: A new residential complex with a load-bearing exoskeleton made from 1,000 tons of raw stone is offering an alternative to carbon-intensive steel and concrete structures. Its designers think that the monumental stone buildings of the past are coming back into fashion
items.text:
From low-carbon concrete to mass timber to green steel , architects across the globe are employing cutting-edge technology to revolutionize eco-friendly building design. But the team behind a new north London apartment complex argues the industry’s path forward may lie in the ways of the past.
With a hulking, pink exoskeleton decorated with Celtic patterns, Petra Heights , a trio of apartment towers ranging from six to 10 stories, looks straight out of the Stone Age . That’s fitting, as the development’s load-bearing structures and decorative cladding are one and the same: stacks of raw, unchiseled stone.
“All of the weight of the building is coming down the stone, and all the wind load is carried by the stone,” the project’s engineer, Steve Webb , co-founder of engineering firm Webb Yates , tells Dezeen ’s Jennifer Hahn. Altogether, the complex houses a ground-floor storefront, two rooftop gardens and 22 apartments.
Petra Heights is part of an ongoing collaboration between architecture firm Groupwork , headed by Amin Taha , and Webb Yates to popularize stone as a viable alternative to steel and cement, which together represent 16 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions.
The stone frame—made of pink basalt from Sicily and larvikite from Norway—produces fewer carbon emissions than traditional steel-and-concrete models. With a stone external frame and a concrete internal frame, the Petra Heights project produced around 30 percent less carbon emissions than a fully steel or concrete alternative, the Guardian ’s Oliver Wainwright reports. Those savings could rise to 95 percent with domestically-mined stone, per Dezeen .
The two men began looking into stone 15 years ago after running into roadblocks while collaborating on a steel frame. A conservation officer pointed them towards stone. Skeptical, they asked a stonemason about the feasibility of building with the material, the Architect's Newspaper ’s Richard Martin reports.
“Are you completely stupid?” Webb recalls the mason saying, according to the Architect’s Newspaper . “Just look around London—it’s been all stone for the last one thousand years. It’s still standing. Of course you can build in stone.”
Since then, they have continually pushed the edge of what stone and wood can do. items.desc: A trust says the river-dwelling mammals could improve the health of the waterway.
items.text:
Beavers could be reintroduced to the River Waveney, like the ones pictured here, that have been living in the River Glaven, Norfolk
A river separating two counties could become home to beavers as work begins to explore where a colony could be introduced.
The River Waveney Trust is in conversation with Natural England and other agencies about potentially reintroducing the river-dwelling mammals along the River Waveney.
The 59-mile (95km) waterway rises in Redgrave and Lopham Fen in Suffolk and heads east, creating a border between Norfolk and Suffolk as it flows out into the River Yare at Great Yarmouth.
Ange Lamb, catchment resilience officer, said the upper reaches of the River Waveney and its tributaries could make ideal environments for beavers. If successful, beavers could return by 2029.
Known as river engineers, beavers were native to Britain but they were hunted to extinction by the end of the 16th century.
Conservationists want to reintroduce them to help boost the health of waterways through their ability to create wetland areas.
But there are concerns, particularly around dams being built in inappropriate places and their ability to destroy trees.
Two beaver babies - or kits - were born in the wild in Norfolk for the first time in 500 years at Pensthorpe Natural Park
Beavers have been reintroduced already in Norfolk at enclosures at Sculthorpe Moor Nature Reserve near Fakenham, Wild Ken Hill near King's Lynn and on the River Glaven near Holt.
A pair of beavers have also been spotted in the wild at Pensthorpe Natural Park, which is a short distance downstream from Sculthorpe Moor.
In Suffolk, a colony was introduced at Little Haugh Hall at Norton, near Bury St Edmunds.
River Waveney Trust is holding a series of events to discuss the proposals and it hopes to engage with local landowners in Bungay, Palgrave and Eye.
Lamb added: "Our aim is to ensure that local communities, landowners, anglers and conservation groups have the opportunity to be part of the discussion from the beginning."
While talks are beginning, Lamb said it would be years before any decision would be made, which would require a licence from Natural England.

items.text:
Unconventional wedding venues can delight and surprise guests—and even the couple. While they may take more planning than a commonly used space (like a church or banquet hall), they often deliver striking visual impact and serve as a unique metaphor for love and devotion. Couple Nara Kim and Yoorim held their nuptials in a rice paddy in Hoengseong, Gangwon-do, South Korea. Part wedding, part art installation , it was all a celebration of love. Photographer Kyungho Lee immortalized the special day in stunning imagery.
The idea to marry in a rice paddy grew out of how Kim and Yoorim viewed their relationship. “The eight years the couple spent together were likened to the process of cultivating the land, sowing seeds, and finally reaping a harvest,” an Instagram post from Ryohan , their wedding director, explains. “Inspired by this, they envisioned a wedding in a rice paddy; after searching for a suitable location for about a month, they ultimately chose this spot in Hoengseong.”
The wedding setup featured long tables centered in the rice paddy clearing. Just beyond one table was the ceremony site, marked by a sculptural backdrop of cascading, braided rice straw punctuated by a variety of flowers. When not in use, the piece served as both art and a monument to Kim and Yorrim’s love.
The ceremony space was prepared by harvesting the rice grown there with a tractor, and the crop became part of the wedding itself. “[The harvested rice] was used to prepare food and tteok (traditional rice cakes) for the guests, while bags of the rice were given as wedding favors—a gesture symbolizing the sharing of the couple’s hard-earned harvest,” Ryohan shares. “Every step of the wedding—from the rice growing in the paddy to its appearance on the guests’ dining tables—was woven into a single, cohesive narrative. Rather than simply decorating nature, the wedding allowed nature itself to become a work of art.”

items.text:
A post shared by Region of Durham Paramedic Services (@durhamparamedic)
Being a paramedic takes a special kind of person. It calls for compassion, resilience, and the ability to stay calm when others are at their most vulnerable. Just one day on the job can take its toll, yet Durham, California-based paramedic Mike Nevill dedicated an incredible 59 years to the vital role. A recent viral video captures a heartwarming tribute made to Nevill as he sits in his ambulance for the last time before retiring.
As Nevill sits in the driver’s seat, he listens to a radio tribute from the dispatch team thanking him for his dedication and reflecting on his extraordinary career. Outside the ambulance, community members gather to show their support, while Nevill appears visibly emotional. The tribute also highlights how Nevill inspired his own daughter to follow in his footsteps and become a paramedic, “carrying forward the Nevill family tradition of caring for others.”
When sharing the video on Instagram , Durham Region Paramedic Services wrote in the caption, “Beginning his career in 1967, Mike dedicated a lifetime to caring for others, serving as a paramedic, supervisor, mentor and leader. His commitment extended beyond Durham, with decades of service in Kawartha Lakes and Northumberland County as well.” They added, “The number of lives Mike has touched throughout his record-breaking career is truly immeasurable. Thank you for your dedication, compassion and commitment to our profession and community.”
People online were quick to share their admiration for Nevill’s decades of service. One person wrote, “59 years of service ??? Paramedics have the hardest of all first responders, dude as a Firefighter my hat is off to you.” Another commented, “59 years as a paramedic! This man should never have to pay for a drink again.”
Let’s hope Nevill can now enjoy a well-deserved rest.

items.text:
2 prominent chemical compounds prohibited under international law over health concerns are being found at substantially lower concentrations in England’s rivers.
Concentrations of these so-called ‘forever chemicals’ falling 30% in water and 49% in fish was “brilliant to see,” one researcher told the BBC , saying it was a marker for “how far we have come.”
For many decades, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS, have been used to create coatings that resist fire, oil, stains, and water. They’re used in products like waterproof clothing, stain-resistant furniture, food packaging, adhesives, cosmetics, firefighting spray foams, medical equipment, and non-stick cooking surfaces.
All that time, however, PFAS were making their way into the environment where because of their unique structure and characteristics, they substantially resist biodegradation, earning them the moniker ‘forever chemicals.’
Two forms of PFAS known as perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctane sulfonic acid, (PFOS) were banned under the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants in almost all products.
The UK being a party to the convention, PFOS was all but banned in the UK in 2010, and PFOA in 2020. France implemented bans of these two chemicals in certain products in January, while the US Environmental Protection Agency announced new drinking water testing regimes for 6 common PFAS in 2024.
Despite this 10 year disparity, concentrations of PFOA in England’s rivers had still fallen 29% compared to 30% for PFOS in the recent test work conducted by the UK Environment Agency (EA).

There are thousands of different PFAS manufactured around the world, but far fewer are used on a wide scale. The EA now routinely tests for 60 forms of PFAS in the country’s rivers, lakes, groundwater, estuaries, coastal waters, fish, and shellfish
The World Health Organization’s Int. Agency for Research on Cancer considers there to be “sufficient” evidence that PFOA is carcinogenic in humans, while research on PFOS suggests this compound is “possibly carcinogenic” in humans.

items.title: The Stories Behind 20 Historic Canals That Changed World Trade And Engineering, Uncovered By This Researcher
items.desc: One stuck ship in the Suez Canal was enough to stall global trade for six days. These canals and waterway feats show how long people have been reshaping rivers and land to keep the world’s goods moving.
items.text:
One problem comes up again and again in this list: how do you move a boat when a waterway rises or falls? The earliest answer was the flash lock, a simple gate that sent vessels through on a sudden surge but wasted supply and created tricky currents. The pound lock changed that by raising or lowering boats inside a closed chamber, while flights of locks tackled steeper climbs one step at a time. In a few places, engineers turned to boat lifts, mechanical giants that carry vessels up and down in water-filled tanks.
Mujtuba points out that these methods didn’t replace one another in a tidy, worldwide progression. Each region chose what suited its terrain, budget, local materials and traffic. “Engineers were not following one inevitable path,” he says. “They were trying to solve local problems with the tools and resources they had.”
That practical spirit is still visible today. Some of these waterways continue to carry freight, while others survive mainly as heritage sites, yet both show how societies once linked farms with cities, mines with factories and inland regions with the sea. Ships, navigation and ports have changed beyond recognition, but the core challenges haven’t: water must be controlled, routes have to stay open, and one blockage in the wrong place can ripple far beyond the canal itself.

81 years ago today, UNESCO was first formed to promote world peace by uniting countries through education, the arts, sciences, and culture. Fostering universal respect for all nations, UNESCO (which stands for United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization) has 193 member states sponsoring projects that improve literacy, provide technical training and education, advance science, and preserve regional and cultural history. READ the major milestone UNESCO just completed in Iraq… (1945)
UNESCO’s largest and most well-known activity is the designation of landmarks that hold cultural or natural importance. These UNESCO World Heritage Sites are masterpieces of human creative genius and landmarks of nature. Designated as ‘patrimony’, with outstanding value to the story of humanity, there have been 1,223 sites protected across 168 countries, so far. Italy is the country with the UNESCO World Heritage Sites (60) with China closely following with 59—and Germany some distance behind at 54. The United States has 26, many of which are natural.
UNESCO has also launched global movements, such as Education For All, to further advance its core objectives of ensuring no child goes uneducated. UNESCO also plays a large role in the protection of monuments and patrimony from destruction, but natural and human-caused. At the time of writing, UNESCO’s ‘Reviving the Spirit of Mosul’ Campaign just completed a landmark restoration in the northern Iraqi city that was once the capital of ISIS.
The famous al-Nuri ‘Leaning Minaret’ of the 12th-century mosque of the same name was just rebuilt with its signature lean intact. Reviving the Spirit of Mosul has also seen over 120 heritage buildings restored from war damage according to the original plan and design of the age in which they were built, and many of them are now not only inhabited by local families, but some by the very craftsmen whose traditional skills informed their reconstruction. (1945)

items.desc: Some of the “very last wild and healthy ecosystems” unblemished by humans have been discovered in the remote atolls of the Pacific Ocean teeming with life. items.text:
Some of the “very last wild and healthy ecosystems” unblemished by humans have been discovered in the remote atolls of the Pacific Ocean teeming with life.
Scientists wrote in a new study that, although humans have left their mark on virtually every place on the planet, a few very remote islands of coral may be the exceptions.
Researchers described the two coral atolls, Bikar and Bokak, located in the territory of the Marshall Islands, to be some of the most intact ecosystems remaining in the region and perhaps the world.
The two atolls—roughly midway between Hawaii and the Philippines—are now part of a newly created National Marine Sanctuary.
“Bikar and Bokak are not just treasures for the Marshall Islands but for the entire planet, a gift from the community of Utirik Atoll, which has traditionally and vigilantly safeguarded these fragile ecosystems for decades,” said study first author Dr. Alan Friedlander.
Bikar and Bokak are the northernmost atolls in the Marshall Islands, lying around 72 and 239 miles from the nearest inhabited atoll, respectively.
The research team in 2023 began conducting extensive monitoring of local land, sea, and sky ecosystems, assessing sea- and shorebird populations, and vegetation.
They conducted surveys of turtle nesting, coral reefs and fish assemblages using scuba, underwater video, deep-sea camera deployments, and a submarine.
Dr. Friedlander, a marine ecologist at the University of Hawai’i, says the extensive surveying of the ecosystems offers an unparalleled glimpse into how they function with only minimal human influence.
Two years after the assessment, some 18,500 square miles around the atolls were declared the country’s first national marine sanctuary.
“These atolls have extensive seabird colonies, mature native vegetation, active turtle nesting, high fish numbers with large predators… and surprisingly diverse and poorly-known deep-sea communities.”
For instance, they counted over a dozen breeding seabird colonies, 266 groups of reef fish, 79 groups of deep-sea fishes, and 15 groups of open-water predators—including sharks, jacks, and wahoo.
Fully 14 of the observed groups haven’t previously been recorded in the Marshall Islands, and two might be species new to science.

122 years ago today, King Gillette patented the disposable safety razor: an enormous improvement over the day’s shaving technology of straight, forged blades that needed to be honed every day with a leather strop. By contrast, Gillette utilized stamped razers from carbon steel sheets, while adapting existing safety features that prevented injury beyond the odd nick. The result, despite being disposable, was both expensive and hugely popular. READ a bit more about this American innovation… (1904)
Gillette first got the idea for a disposable razor when a friend pointed out that disposable products guarantee future customer purchases. Gillette’s razor retailed for a substantial $5 (equivalent to $175.00 in 2024)—half the average working man’s weekly pay—yet sold by the millions.
In 2020, Gillette announced a commitment to reduce the use of virgin (unrecycled) plastics by 50% by 2030 and maintain zero waste to landfill status across all plants.
9 years ago, Pakistani archeologists revealed to the world the finished excavations of the Bhamala Stupa , one of the oldest in the world, and a monumental work of the Buddhist faith that contains a depiction of Buddha sometimes described as “sleeping,” but he’s actually in Samadhi. The site has received UNESCO World Heritage status, and was discovered in the early 20th century, but excavations were halted in the 30s.
Located in the far north of Pakistan, the stupa is part of the overall Bhamala Stupa Complex which includes monastic quarters and other buildings. Many important statuary works have been uncovered there.
It’s dated to between the 2nd and 5th centuries CE, and is considered to be the final evolution of the stupa building style of the Gandhara civilization. (2017)

items.text:
Annual display appears to radiate from constellation of Leo in eastern sky as Earth passes through comet debris stream
T he annual Leonid meteor shower reaches its peak this week, offering a chance to count meteors. The shower is expected to be at its most active during the night of 17–18 November. Under ideal conditions, observers may see up to 10–15 meteors an hour.
What they lack in numbers, they make up for in brilliance.
The Leonids are produced by dust shed by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the Sun every 33 years. As Earth passes through this debris stream, the particles strike our atmosphere at about 71 km/s, making them among the fastest meteors of any annual shower. As a result, they often leave bright, fleeting streaks across the sky.
The meteors appear to radiate from the constellation of Leo, the lion, which rises in the east after midnight. The chart shows the view looking east from London at midnight on 17–18 November.
Conditions will improve towards dawn as Leo climbs higher in the sky. As an added reward for your efforts, Mars and Jupiter will form a beautiful pair just in front of Leo’s chest.
From the southern hemisphere, Leo remains relatively low in the northern sky, making the hours before dawn the best time to look for meteors.

items.title: Met Office yellow warning in place as snow could disrupt Tuesday morning travel
items.desc: Snow could bring some transport disruption to the hills of northern England and southern Scotland, as Chris Fawkes explains.
items.text:
Snow brought traffic to a standstill on the A66 in February
Parts of northern England and southern Scotland are set to get an early taste of winter as hill snow moves in on Tuesday.
A Met Office yellow warning for snow is valid until midday Tuesday with 5-15cm expected at some locations above 300-400m.
Major routes like the A74(M), A66 and M62 could all have problems with transport disruption.
Some railways are also likely to be affected with longer journey times for train services.
Cold health alerts are also in place , external for northern England issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) until 09:00 GMT on Thursday.
The Met Office has issued a yellow snow warning for Tuesday
A weather front is pushing north and east across the UK bringing a spell of rain to many areas. As this rain reaches northern England it will encounter a reservoir of colder and drier air.
Some of the rain will evaporate in this drier air, which will cool the atmosphere further by a process known as evaporative cooling - the same process involved in cooling your body down when you sweat.
Eventually rain will start to turn to snow, initially over higher hills in the Pennines, moving to lower hills with time. As the precipitation moves northwards and eastwards, the snow will spread to the Cumbrian hills and into Scotland's Southern Uplands.
The snow will come down in big, wet, chunky flakes which could stick to powerlines and tree branches.
The extra weight of the snow combined with wind gusts of 40-50mph over high ground could bring down tree branches and powerlines, bringing an additional risk of some localised power cuts.

items.title: Europe's Hera Spacecraft Has Begun Its Close-Up Investigation of the Asteroid System NASA Intentionally Hit in 2022
items.desc: The European Space Agency's mission will provide valuable data about the aftermath of the planned collision, which can inform planetary defense measures and reveal insights about asteroids
items.text:
The European Space Agency (ESA) has started its close-up investigation of an asteroid system smashed by NASA in 2022.
ESA’s Hera spacecraft reached the Didymos binary asteroid system on November 4, more than two years after it launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida. The mission will examine the aftermath of NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) collision, helping scientists better understand how the technique could one day be used to protect Earth from incoming space rocks.
The asteroid Didymos is roughly 2,560 feet in diameter and has a companion moonlet called Dimorphos, which is about 495 feet in diameter. They form a binary asteroid system , a pair of asteroids that are gravitationally bound, orbiting each other around a shared center of mass.
In September 2022, the golf-cart-size DART spacecraft intentionally struck the smaller celestial body in the world’s first demonstration of asteroid deflection technology. The mission not only successfully collided with Dimorphos, shortening its orbit around its big sibling by 33 minutes; it also altered the asteroid pair’s route around the sun . Now, Hera is returning to the crash scene to follow up on that work.
“Hera wants to be the detective, like Inspector Colombo, going back to the crash scene,” Patrick Michel , a planetary scientist at the French National Center for Scientific Research and Hera’s principal investigator, tells Meghan Bartels for Space.com .
The spacecraft, which is about the size of a small car , performed its first arrival maneuver on October 15, and ESA released Hera’s first close-up photo of the asteroid duo on November 5. The picture, snapped about 37 miles from the rocky pair, prominently features Didymos, with the smaller Dimorphos mostly hidden in the larger asteroid’s shadow.
While looking at this image, “the first thing we said was wow!” Michel says in a statement . “This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART’s camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world.”
On November 12, ESA released another image of the asteroid system , this time taken from about 35 miles away. It shows one side of Didymos and a sliver of Dimorphos peeking out from behind the larger rock, on the upper left. This photo reveals various features on the bigger asteroid’s surface, including large boulders, smooth areas and a sharp ridge at the equator.

items.desc: The heroic wartime bravery of a British shopkeeper who hid Allied commandos from the Nazis during WWII has been revealed 40 years after her death. Ada Le Poidevin was living on the island of Guernsey in the English Channel when she sheltered three British soldiers left behind during a raid on the Nazi-occupied land in […] The post Heroic Bravery of Woman who Hid Troops from Nazis in WWII Revealed
items.text:
The heroic wartime bravery of a British shopkeeper who hid Allied commandos from the Nazis during WWII has been revealed 40 years after her death.
Ada Le Poidevin was living on the island of Guernsey in the English Channel when she sheltered three British soldiers left behind during a raid on the Nazi-occupied land in 1940.
Despite German troops living next door, she decided to help Corporal Dennis Dumper, Pvt. Fred Drain, and Pvt. Andrew Ross who were stranded without food or shelter.
Ada and her husband Walter offered their garden shed for them to hide in, despite severe consequences if the trio were to be discovered.
All three survived the conflict and they remained close to Ada and Walter, regularly returning to Guernsey to visit them and even attending the couple’s Golden Wedding celebration.
It was the second time Ada had put herself in danger during wartime. During WWI, she spent two years supporting British troops in France working in camps that came under enemy fire—and suffered heavy damage.
Now her story has been pieced together by her niece Liz Walton, using a treasure trove of diaries, photographs, and records she inherited.
“There were huge risks because there were Germans living next door and people were being sent off to concentration camps, said the 79-year-old Walton. “They were terrified of being caught.”
“It must have been absolutely horrendous for people like my aunt, who had been involved in the first World War, and then 20 years later to have the Germans actually in their homes.”
Liz, a retired teacher from Guernsey, turned into a detective to match her aunt’s personal accounts and photos with official wartime records.
She had been fascinated by Ada’s stories since childhood until she died at the age of 88—of ordinary people sacrificing during extraordinary times.
Ada was born in 1895 in Guernsey (30 miles west of the coastline of Normandy, France), and volunteered for the Salvation Army in France in 1917, while in her early 20s.
“There were no men in our family that could go and fight,” Liz said. “She felt a calling to go.”
Ada spent two years in British camps, providing refreshments to soldiers, writing letters for them, and mending their clothes—at sites being fired upon more than once.
For four years after the war, she helped bereaved families travel to France to visit the graves of loved ones killed during the conflict.

items.title: How to spot November's planetary parade in the pre-dawn sky
items.desc: The planets of Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will align in pre-dawn sky throughout November.
items.text:
Stargazers are being treated to a diagonal parade of four planets in the pre-dawn sky throughout November.
Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will all be visible to the naked eye in the south-eastern to eastern sky.
Particularly notable will be the line-up on Monday 16 November when Mars and Jupiter will appear exceptionally close together, according to the Royal Museums Greenwich.
From 24 November, a full Moon - the first of a run of four supermoons - will also join the planets in the morning sky.
Mercury will be the hardest planet to spot in the parade.
As the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest in our solar system, it is permanently locked in solar glare.
It is only visible in twilight and never in a fully dark sky. As always it will be dim and close to the horizon.
Try spotting it in a wide open sky with a flat horizon and look to the south-east.
Venus shines in the night sky above a waxing crescent Moon
Above Mercury and toward the right, you will spot Venus.
Venus is an easy planet to find as it is the brightest object in our night sky after the Moon. It has the highest albedo of any major planet in our solar system - that is reflects more sunlight back into space thus appearing brighter.
It is also usually the closest planet to Earth in its orbit - a mere 24 million miles away at times. It is a similar size too.
It will be higher in the sky than Mercury and visible earlier in the night in the hours before sunrise.
Don't mistake it with the bright star Spica which will be close to it. Stars twinkle while planets glow steadily.
Mars and Jupiter will appear to be very close to each other in the sky on the 15 and 16 November.
Mars is currently high in the eastern sky, with Jupiter below but appearing brighter.
"They will be separated by just 1.2 degrees, or roughly the width of a finger held at arm's length," according to Gideon Bendavid-Walker, astronomer at the Royal Observatory Greenwich.
The two planets will appear close to the bright star Regulus and may even look like a triple star.
If you have binoculars or a telescope then a few other bonus planets will also be visible this month.
At a similar time before sunrise, Uranus will be setting in the west. Then Saturn and Neptune will also be visible for a time in the evening rather than the morning sky.
To view the parade, find a spot away from light pollution with a good view of the eastern horizon and let your eyes adjust to the dark for around twenty minutes.

items.text:
From the sun-soaked plains of Parma comes the story of an Italian farmer who accidentally brought on a Biblical resurrection with very modern implications for our food system.
Claudio Grossi doubted whether the shriveled wheat seeds he found in his attic would grow into anything.
It didn’t take long for Grossi to forget that he threw the seeds into a pile of manure for curiosity’s sake. When the growing season got going, however, he witnessed these decades-old seeds grow into something entirely unexpected—something ancient.
Smithsonian Magazine’s Lina Zeldovich wrote that Grossi looked on with surprise as what was obviously a kind of wheat began to tower over his commercially-raised yellow wheat, and that rather than a single ear, these seeds preserved by his great-grandfather sprouted 7.
The pattern of those 7 ears proved important. One tall ear was surrounded by 6 thin ears of different colors. Grossi had spent his whole life farming wheat and had never heard of anything like it. Though he could find nothing about it in any agricultural manuals, a clue as to the “freak” grain’s origin did indeed come from a Good Book.
“And behold, seven ears of grain came up upon one stalk, rank and good,” read a page in the Book of Genesis that Grossi happened upon one Sunday in church. 7 ears, one stalk, just like the “freak of nature” at his farm.
Indeed, what his great-grandfather grew after he bought the farm in Italy’s Emilia-Romagna region in 1915 was an ancient form of wheat called Triticum turgidum convar. compositum, as scientists at the University of Parma would later determine. It evolved in Türkiye, Egypt, and other countries along the Mediterranean, and was cultivated one upon a time in Italy.
As a commercial grain, its production declined around the time of the Mussolini dictatorship because its impressive height made it vulnerable to snapping under wind, heavy rains, and hailstorms before the grains would mature.
Additionally, dough made from T. turgidum flour doesn’t leaven well, and unusual preparations need to be made for baking with it.
Yet one by one, the positives which Grossi experienced made him wonder why Italian farmers ever stopped cultivating it. Tall, large, and hardy, it overshadows weeds, shows resistance to drought, and appears less reliant on fertilizer than other breeds. Grossi began calling it his “Miracle Wheat” or grano del miracolo.

items.title: Extreme weather leaves gardeners hedging their bets
items.desc: Gardeners across Sussex are changing their planting strategies after this year's unprecedented heat.
items.text:
Plants and trees from hotter parts of the world are being brought into Sussex
Gardeners in one of the most drought-hit parts of the UK have said they are adapting their planting strategies amid increasingly extreme weather.
West Sussex - like most of the country - experienced an unprecedented summer marked by record-breaking heatwaves and severe drought.
The conditions have put immense stress on many traditional plant species, with some seriously struggling or dying completely.
Iain Parkinson, head of landscape and horticulture at Kew Wakehurst near Ardingly, said he had seen a "big change" in climate over the some 40 years he has worked there.
Meanwhile, senior gardener at High Beeches near Haywards Heath, Elliot Chandler, said some rhododendrons had died off this year.
"That's probably going to continue," he said.
"We'll do what we can for the plants...but if they're not surviving, then we need to plant different things.
"That's the only way we can really maintain the garden and keep it full of interest and flowers."
This year's heat and lack of rainfall were unprecedented
Joe Whelan, head gardener at Nymans in Handcross, warned another year of drought could be "quite detrimental" on larger, more mature trees.
The gardeners said planting a greater diversity of species will be key to climate resilience, with plants from North America, southeastern Europe, central Asia, South Korea and Japan potentially faring better in future.
Chandler added it will not be a case of ripping out old plants and planting new species "in one go" but rather a gradual change over time with a "really diverse mix of things".
Whelan said it will be difficult to predict what will do well in the future.
It will be about "experimenting and accepting that some things probably aren't going to make it", he continued.

items.title: National Trust takes back land for nature restoration
items.desc: The trust hopes to restore the site, create new wildlife habitats and improve access to green space.
items.text:
The National Trust hopes to create new wildlife habitats to attract wildlife including water vole and turtle doves
A 370-acre (150-hectare) area of land on the edge of Cambridge has been returned to the care of the National Trust - for the first time in 60 years.
The area - known as Northfield - runs alongside the opposite side of Quy Road towards Bottisham, seven miles (11km) from the city and close to Anglesey Abbey.
The National Trust hopes to restore the natural site to create new wildlife habitats and improve community access to green space.
Emma Ormond-Bones, general manager of the National Trust's North Cambridgeshire Portfolio, said: "We want Northfield to become a place where nature can thrive, helping wildlife recover and building resilience to a changing climate."
The project comes at a time when Cambridgeshire remains one of the most nature-depleted counties in the UK, where demand for accessible green space is increasing as the county's population rapidly grows.
Northfield is a rich natural site with a distinctive fen-edge landscape where low-lying fenland meets the higher chalk ridge
Northfield has been acquired by the trust for the first time since the 1960s, following an agreement with the tenants.
The site has a rich natural and cultural heritage as well as a chalk stream, with the trust describing the area as "a distinctive fen-edge landscape where low-lying fenland meets the higher chalk ridge".
There is evidence of human activity on the site stretching back thousands of years including the Roman period.
The National Trust said it hoped that, over time, species such as harvest mice, water voles and turtle doves would benefit.
Northfield is the first project within the trust's new masterplan for the area, which forms part of a wider Wicken Fen Vision and long-term initiative to "create a more connected and resilient landscape for wildlife and people stretching from Wicken Fen to the edge of Cambridge".
Ormond-Bones added: "Northfield has the potential to deliver meaningful benefit to both people and wildlife and we want local people to play a vital role in helping shape what that future will look like."
The charity said it was keen to understand what mattered most to local people and how the site would become a place people felt connected to, valued and enjoyed for generations to come.

items.title: Climate action discussed at youth COP meeting
items.desc: School children gather to discuss climate issues to coincide with the COP31 conference in Turkey.
items.text:
Dorset was hit by widespread flooding earlier this year
School children are taking part in an event aimed at inspiring climate action, to coincide with the COP31 international climate conference in Turkey.
Hosted at the Kingston Maurwood campus, the first Dorset-wide Youth COP has brought children from 14 schools together to discuss issues including future careers.
Maria Clarke, of Dorset Local Nature Partnership, said young people should be "given a voice" over dealing with climate change.
A Dorset COP 2026 event is also being held on Saturday as world leaders and delegates gather at Antalya in Turkey for the COP31 climate summit.
The Dorset Youth COP event includes discussions about how young people feel about climate change as well as a panel session introducing them to the range of jobs and careers in the climate and energy sectors.
Maria Clarke, of Dorset Local Nature Partnership, said: "Young people are inheriting the climate and ecological emergencies that previous generations have created and need to be given a voice in jointly developing and implementing the solutions to these issues."
"The Youth COP aims to raise awareness, inspire and support them to take action now and into the future."
The main Dorset COP 2026 event takes place on Saturday also at the Kingston Maurward Campus near Dorchester.
The fourth annual event brings together community groups, environmental organisations, experts and political leaders.
The programme will explore how Dorset can respond to climate change, nature loss, food resilience, pollution and other environmental challenges.
The programme will also feature an exhibition of over 30 local organisations and a Question Time-style panel bringing together Dorset MPs, council leaders and independent climate experts.
Giles Watts, chair of Dorset CAN said the event's focus was on making "a lasting positive impact" on climate and nature local areas.
"We want to bring people together, listen to different perspectives and energise local communities and politicians to act more quickly on the pressing challenges we face," he added.

items.desc: Archivist Discovers Rare Photo of Abraham Lincoln at Gettysburg Nearly a Century Later For nearly 90 years, a damaged glass plate negative concealed a remarkable piece of American history. items.text:
Portrait of Abraham Lincoln. (Photo: PHOTOGRAPHER/AUTHOR'S NAME via Wikimedia Commons , Public domain)
For nearly 90 years, a damaged glass plate negative concealed a remarkable piece of American history. Cataloged as a crowd scene, the photograph showed spectators gathered around a platform in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. In 1952, archivist Josephine Cobb enlarged the image and discovered Abraham Lincoln standing among the crowd. The photograph captured the president at the dedication of the Soldiers’ National Cemetery on November 19, 1863, the same day he delivered the Gettysburg Address.
Cobb joined the U.S. National Archives in 1936. Her work focused on historical photographs, including Civil War images. When she examined the glass plate, she suspected it might depict the Gettysburg ceremony. A tall flag helped her locate the speakers’ platform. She then enlarged that section to examine the figures more closely.
The result revealed a small, bare-headed man with a beard and a distinctive profile. Cobb identified him as Lincoln. She also recognized Ward Hill Lamon, the president’s bodyguard and the ceremony’s chief marshal, along with Pennsylvania Governor Andrew Curtin. Other figures have been proposed as members of Lincoln’s party, though some identifications remain disputed.
The photograph belonged to a collection associated with Civil War photographer Mathew Brady . The U.S. government purchased Brady’s photographic collection in the 1870s, and the material eventually entered the National Archives. However, the photographer who took this particular image remains unknown. The glass plate had also lost roughly a quarter of its upper-left corner, further complicating its examination.
Cobb estimated that the photograph was taken around noon, when Lincoln arrived at the platform. His famous address came approximately three hours later. The image does not capture the speech itself. Instead, it offers a rare glimpse of Lincoln at the ceremony before he delivered one of the most enduring speeches in American history.
The discovery became public on February 12, 1953, Lincoln’s birthday. The Gettysburg Times reported the finding, and Life magazine later published the image. Early coverage approached the identification cautiously because the figure’s face was blurred. Lincoln occupies only a small portion of the original photograph, making historical context essential to the identification.
Cobb’s discovery reflected years of experience examining archival images.

items.text:

The lives of artists Duncan Grant and Vanessa Bell —collaborators, companions and sometimes lovers—were deeply intertwined both on canvases and in private quarters.
The pair were central figures in the Bloomsbury Group , a circle of artists and intellectuals active in early 20th-century Britain who radically, and often controversially, challenged contemporary creative and social norms. These included public sentiments on philosophy, sexuality and mental illness. The group featured, among others, the economist John Maynard Keynes , as well as the writers E. M. Forster and Virginia Woolf , Bell’s biological sister.
Grant and Bell were often the subjects of each other’s work. Among their most well-known collaborations is one of Grant’s first and most extravagant depictions of Bell, a full-length portrait painted in 1915.
But this summer, while preparing for “ Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury ,” an exhibition that opened this week at Tate Britain, scholars discovered an intimate, previously unknown work that sheds new light on the end of Grant and Bell’s relationship.
Hidden for some 60 years among private family papers, the newly recovered drawing is thought to be Grant’s final depiction of Bell. items.text:
What began as an exciting hiking trip quickly turned into something else entirely when climbers in Greece found an orphaned seal pup on a beach at the bottom of a cliff.
Considered a Critically Endangered species in Greece, the climbers resolved to go right back up the way they came—the seal pup safely secured in a backpack.
It was stranded without its mother on the inaccessible Kalamia Beach—whose beauty and solitude were supposed to be the climbers’ reward for negotiating the rugged cliffs on the island of Kythira.
Vrettos Sklavos, from Outdoor Activities Greece said there is a sea cave near Kalamia Beach that these Mediterranean monk seals use to escape rough seas. Perhaps a big wave had separated the little fellow from its mother.
An animal rescue operation on the island wrote on Facebook that the climbers took “all the right steps,” calling (MOm) the Hellenic Society for the Study and Protection of the Mediterranean Monk Seal, the coast guard, and Animal Aid Kythira , whose veterinarians eventually descended the cliffs together with the climbers to rescue the seal.
“A huge thank you to Vrettos and his team for their immediate response,” the operation wrote on Facebook.
In an update from Keep Talking Greece , the seal is said to have arrived severely dehydrated and malnourished, weighing just 15 kilograms at 1 year old. It was determined that after a brief stay with Animal Aid Kythira it would be transported to Thessaly on the mainland before eventually arriving at the Society’s rehabilitation location in Spata.
Here, it will receive round-the-clock care with the aim of attempting to preserve enough of its wild intuition and nature as to permit a return to the sea when the time is right.

items.title: Summer heatwave put bin crews lives at risk, says council worker
items.desc: Crews faced a "perfect storm" of challenges during the UK's record-breaking weather, it's claimed.
items.text:
Some bin collections were missed partly because of the heatwave
Some bin collections were missed over the summer in a county partly because the heatwave became so serious it posed a risk to the lives of workers, a council worker has said.
Flintshire County Council's Chris Goddard said crews faced a "perfect storm" of challenges during the UK's record-breaking hot weather , causing a spate of widespread missed collections.
During the summer, drought was declared in all of Wales and wildfires caused devastation in parts of the country .
Goddard said: "We do have to make some difficult decisions but ultimately if there is a fatality in the workplace because of a decision I've made, that's something that I would have to live with - and probably defend."
Despite the missed collections the council remained on target to hit the Welsh government's national 70% waste recycling target this year, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said.
Flintshire County Council is on track to hit its waste recycling target despite the disruption
Goddard, the council's streetscene service manager, said: "We had maybe five or six operational challenges that all came at the same time in a perfect storm this summer.
"Unfortunately, the heatwave was one of them and it was a contributing factor. We do have to prioritise staff safety above all else.
"My number one job every day is to make sure that everybody goes home safely and we take that really seriously within streetscene. That was only one of several contributing factors.
"That level of change is naturally going to cause a few bumps in the road, particularly with staff being asked to do a little bit more. There were some staffing issues during that period too."
Councillors praised Flintshire residents for largely embracing three-weekly residual waste collections and ensuring that the authority remained on-target to hit its statutory recycling rate.
"Three-weekly was very controversial at the time it came in," said Saltney councillor Richard Lloyd.
"It's quite clear to see now that the three-weekly black bin collection has been a good new factor. Recycling has improved at the kerbside."
Councillors said in the authority's meeting the change to three-weekly bin collections meant the council should still hit target despite the disruption.
The council also cut the amount of waste it sent to landfill or Parc Adfer by 6,467.49 tonnes between 2024 and 2026, and that improvement continued this year despite problems this summer.

VHILS uses acid, oxidation, and subtraction to transform corroded metal into layered compositions. The works bring together visual traces of Lisbon, São Paulo, and Shanghai. A large-scale intervention on the gallery’s glass facade also extends the exhibition into the surrounding city.
Since beginning his career in graffiti in the early 2000s, VHILS has expanded his practice to include bas-relief carving, metal etching, wood carving, sculpture, and site-specific installations. His work considers what is lost as cities change, particularly as globalization and development threaten established communities. After more than a decade of working with Brazilian communities, he returns to São Paulo with these questions at the center of his latest exhibition.
Atrito: Arqueologia do Presente opens on November 14 and runs through February 20, 2027 at Galleria Continua São Paulo.

items.desc: Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw gas field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty.
items.text:
The Jackdaw platform is located 150 miles east of Aberdeen
Gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field, with the UK energy secretary saying it will help to heat millions of homes and businesses this winter.
Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty and a court case.
It has now been announced that it has begun producing gas which will start flowing into Britain, according to its operator Adura.
The UK government approved production from the gas field in the North Sea last month, amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "Last month, I gave Jackdaw the green light and today its gas will start flowing into Britain, thanks to the hard work of the skilled North Sea workers.
"It means homegrown gas from this project will help to heat millions of British homes and businesses this winter and beyond, in a boost for our energy security.
"It also will help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission gas as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear."

items.text:
Tirana, Albania, has become one of Europe’s fastest-growing cities. This growth has sparked a real estate boom, but locals worry about losing green areas and public spaces. Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) has addressed these issues with its proposal for an upcoming development on Rinia Park, in the heart of Tirana.
Named Fountain Plaza Tirana, the project won over designs presented by four other international firms. Conceived as a mixed-use building, Fountain Plaza Tirana will stand several feet above Rinia Park, preserving and expanding the public park area while making room for a new hotel, apartments, offices, and cultural spaces.
The building evokes a dense cloud formation above the park. To achieve this, layers of rounded, perforated white terraces rest on slim columns, while two wider structures at opposite ends of the building house the elevators that provide floor access. To avoid breaking with the “floating” concept, these elements are clad in flute glass to let light shine through and onto the park.
“We have reimagined urban living in three dimensions—not as a vertical extrusion or a tower competing for attention on the skyline, but as a cloud of homes hovering above the park,” said BIG founder Bjarke Ingels told Dezeen . “Rather than diminishing the park or displacing public life, the building enhances and accommodates both.”
As such, Fountain Plaza Tirana will also feature an open-access library, a covered public auditorium, and community facilities. In addition to the design that lets pedestrians move freely across the park, this aims to make the building’s ground floor a bustling gathering place for city dwellers and visitors alike.
The design also accounts for Tirana’s weather, particularly its hot summers. The structures bring shade to a public park without completely blocking sunlight. Meanwhile, the water features, described as an “inverted fountain,” can cool the area with the effect of a light drizzle. The water used comes from a closed-loop system. With this, the water collected from the building and the green areas at the bottom is stored, filtered, and returned to the park below.
While a building timeline has yet to be announced, it will surely be interesting to see how Fountain Plaza Tirana takes shape. items.text:
From the first day of his life, little infant Adnan has suffered a seizure roughly every 13 minutes.
One can only imagine the reactions from his Dubai hospital bedside when, having received a still-experimental drug, his seizures stopped for the day.
And for the week, and the week after that—and the week after that.
The story comes via the Khaleej Times , which reported that the Dubai Health Authority (DHA) granted an application from King’s College Hospital London in Dubai through a “compassionate use” pathway for the use of a drug that is otherwise not approved for commercial use.
Called ABS-1230, the experimental oral medication targets abnormal activity in an ion channel associated with the “extremely rare” form of genetic epilepsy Adnan suffers from.
According to data from the treatment’s developer, Adnan is the youngest patient in the world to receive ABS-1230 and only the second infant to be given the experimental medication.
At the Dubai hospital, sequencing of Adnan’s entire genome revealed a gene variant associated with the seizures and allowed the medical team to identify ABS-1230 as a potential treatment option.
Led by Professor Ubaid Shah, consultant pediatric neurologist and epileptologist at the hospital, the drug was administered on September 14th. The success was so profound and immediate that Adnan was discharged from the hospital with his family just a week later, without a single seizure having been recorded during that time.
“This is an exceptional moment for us, and it highlights what precision medicine can achieve when we are able to identify the genetic cause of a disease and choose a treatment that targets the mechanism linked to it,” Professor Shah told the Times.
Adnan suffered no clinical seizures at his October 11th follow-up. The hospital said he continues to be seizure-free as of November 2nd, and the infant is finally beginning to pass some early development milestones.
“Despite the encouraging response, we will continue to monitor his condition closely to assess whether the results are sustained and whether the experimental treatment is safe,” Professor Shah said.
Indeed, Shah and his colleagues stressed that the treatment is still experimental and requires more research before it can be approved for use by the public. That being said, however, Adnan’s response to it couldn’t have been more positive.

items.text:
Video games get a bad rap. Though they’re often looked down upon as a distracting outlet for young adults, despite the creativity and problem-solving that’s often involved, it turns out they can also be essential in saving lives. Teenager Kylie Arellano was rescued after allegedly being held captive for more than 500 days, thanks to an unlikely connection she made with another player through the popular online game Among Us .
An online multiplayer game that uses social deduction to seek out the “impostors” in a group of players, Among Us rose in popularity during the COVID-19 pandemic and served as a great way for friends to keep in touch during quarantine. For Arellano, who went missing from her Utah home in May 2025, the game’s ability to connect players with one another ultimately became a crucial part of her rescue.
Arellano was allegedly held captive in the basement of 39-year-old Adam Hunter Harmel’s home in Huntington, Oregon. Although Harmel had reportedly taken away her original phone, he eventually gave her another device that could connect to Wi-Fi but had no cellular service. This allowed Arellano to play Among Us and, more importantly, communicate with other people through the game.
In mid-October 2026, Arellano began talking with another player she met while playing Among Us . Their conversations eventually moved to another social media platform, where she revealed her identity and explained that she was being held against her will. The other player (a child) told their mother, who contacted the FBI.
On November 1, the FBI monitored a video call between Arellano and the other player’s family, during which she shared details about her situation. Authorities were able to rescue her from the Oregon home that same day. Harmel was subsequently charged with transporting a minor across state lines with the intent to engage in criminal sexual activity.
While Among Us was originally designed as a way for players to work together and identify hidden impostors, for Arellano, it became something much more important. The game provided her with a way to reach the outside world, ultimately helping bring her captivity to an end.
